title: Post-Quantum Succinct Arguments: Breaking the Quantum Rewinding Barrier
authors: Alessandro Chiesa (EPFL & UC Berkeley, Switzerland), Fermi Ma (UC Berkeley & Simons Institute), Nicholas Spooner (Boston University), Mark Zhandry (Princeton & NTT Research)
abstract: We prove that Kilian's four-message succinct argument system is post-quantum secure in the standard model when instantiated with any probabilistically checkable proof and any collapsing hash function (which in turn exist based on the post-quantum hardness of Learning with Errors). This yields the first post-quantum succinct argument system from any falsifiable assumption. At the heart of our proof is a new quantum rewinding procedure that enables a reduction to repeatedly query a quantum adversary for accepting transcripts as many times as desired. Prior techniques were limited to a constant number of accepting transcripts.

A. Our Results

Abstract—We prove that Kilian’s four-message succinct argument system is post-quantum secure in the standard model
when instantiated with any probabilistically checkable proof and
any collapsing hash function (which in turn exist based on the
post-quantum hardness of Learning with Errors). This yields the
ﬁrst post-quantum succinct argument system from any falsiﬁable
assumption.
At the heart of our proof is a new quantum rewinding procedure that enables a reduction to repeatedly query a quantum
adversary for accepting transcripts as many times as desired.
Prior techniques were limited to a constant number of accepting
transcripts.
Index Terms—succinct arguments; post-quantum cryptography; quantum rewinding

In this work, we present a quantum rewinding technique that
enables recording the adversary’s responses on any number of
challenges, with essentially no loss of security. This opens
the door to quantum security for many tasks. Our primary
application is to prove that Kilian’s four-message succinct
argument system for NP is secure against quantum attackers
(assuming the post-quantum hardness of the Learning with
Errors problem). This is the ﬁrst construction of a postquantum succinct argument that is secure under any falsiﬁable
assumption.
Kilian’s protocol uses a collision-resistant hash function
(CRHF) to transform a probabilistically checkable proof (PCP)
into an interactive argument.2 By choosing an appropriate
PCP (e.g., [5]), the resulting argument has communication
complexity and veriﬁer runtime that is polylogarithmic in
the size of the NP witness — an exponential improvement
over standard NP veriﬁcation. The classical security reduction
rewinds the adversary an arbitrary polynomial number of
times, which is completely out of reach of prior rewinding
techniques. Our new rewinding technique allows us to carry
this reduction over to the quantum setting provided the CRHF
used in the protocol satisﬁes a quantum-binding property
called “collapsing” [3]; such hash functions are implied by
the quantum-hardness of Learning with Errors [6].

I. I NTRODUCTION
Will cryptography survive quantum adversaries? Postquantum cryptographic primitives provide part of the answer:
building blocks like one-way functions, hash functions, and
symmetric and public-key encryption can all be built from
post-quantum assumptions. But what about the security of
interactive protocols? While some protocols directly inherit
the post-quantum security of the underlying assumptions,
many classical cryptosystems are proved secure by rewinding
an interactive adversary to record its responses to multiple
different challenges.1 Unfortunately, classical rewinding is
inapplicable if the adversary is running a quantum algorithm,
since measuring the response can irreversibly disturb the
adversary’s state.
While limited techniques for rewinding a quantum adversary
are known [2], [3], [4], the resulting reduction incurs a security
loss exponential in the number of rewinds. These techniques
do sufﬁce to prove security of protocols where the number
of rewinds required is a constant (such as certain sigma
protocols), but unfortunately, this loss results in a reduction
that is far from tight. Even worse, if the classical reduction
requires more than a constant number of rewinds, then the
resulting quantum reduction is useless since it succeeds with
only negligible probability.

Theorem I.1 (Informal). Kilian’s protocol is a post-quantum
succinct argument when instantiated with a collapsing hash
function. Moreover, if the underlying PCP is a proof of knowledge, Kilian’s protocol is a post-quantum succinct argument

protocol refers to any public-coin interactive argument with the
guarantee that any prover that only gives accepting responses
cannot detect if its last response is measured. In particular, we
show the following general result.

B. Our approach
We ﬁrst recall the notion of a rewinding reduction, and
explain why it presents difﬁculties in the quantum setting. For
simplicity, we consider sigma protocols; a transcript of such
a protocol is of the form (a, c, z), where c is the veriﬁer’s
challenge. (Kilian’s protocol is not strictly a sigma protocol,
but the following discussion applies essentially unchanged.)
A rewinding reduction takes an adversary which succeeds in
the protocol with sufﬁciently high probability (i.e., on a large
enough fraction of the challenge space) and obtains accepting
transcripts (a, c1 , z1 ), . . . , (a, ck , zk ) with the same ﬁrst prover
message a but different challenges ci .
Classically, rewinding reductions are straightforward: we
can store the adversary’s state S after it sends a and then
ask it different challenges ci , “rewinding” its state back to S
in between each query. In the quantum setting, on the other
hand, obtaining transcripts requires measuring the adversary’s
response to a challenge, which will irreversibly disturb the
adversary’s (quantum) state. In particular, this may cause
the probability that the adversary is able to answer other
challenges to decrease. If this probability becomes too small,
the adversary will no longer be useful for obtaining accepting
transcripts.
Prior work [2], [3], [4] showed that if the protocol is
collapsing the effect of this disturbance can be bounded. In
particular, if the adversary’s initial success probability is ε, the
probability that we can obtain answers to k random challenges
in sequence is at least ε2k−1 . Unfortunately, this is not enough
to prove post-quantum security for succinct arguments, since
these require k to be super-constant; furthermore, we show
that this bound is actually tight.
The starting point of our work is to observe that if we had
a method of restoring the success probability of the adversary
after each measurement, this would allow us to rewind an
unbounded number of times, similar to the classical setting.
Our main technical contribution is designing an algorithm that
achieves this.
At a high level, the algorithm operates as follows. We
identify a space of states S such that (a) if the adversary’s
state is in S, then it succeeds with good probability, and (b) if
the adversary succeeds with good probability, the projection
of its state on to S is not too small. If we had an efﬁcient
projection ΠS on to S, then we could restore the success

II. T ECHNIQUES
A. Kilian’s protocol
Kilian’s protocol compiles any probabilistically checkable
proof (PCP) into an interactive protocol using a Merkle
tree built from a collision-resistant hash function. A PCP
is an NP proof that can be veriﬁed by reading only a few
random positions [5], [10], [11], [12]. The collision-resistant
hash function enables the argument prover to send a succinct
Merkle tree commitment to the PCP that it can later open on
any subset of positions with a short opening proof.
1) The protocol: Let (PPCP , VPCP ) be a PCP proof system
for an NP relation R, and let {Hλ }λ be a family of collisionresistant hash functions. The argument prover P and argument
veriﬁer V both receive as input the security parameter λ
and an instance x, while the prover additionally receives a
corresponding witness w (such that (x, w) ∈ R). They interact
as follows.
1) V samples a collision-resistant hash function hCRHF ← Hλ
and sends it to P .

2) P computes a PCP string π ← PPCP (x, w), uses
hCRHF to generate a Merkle tree commitment cm ←
Merkle.Commit(hCRHF , π) to π, and sends cm to V .
3) V samples random coins r ← R for the PCP veriﬁer VPCP
and sends them to P .
4) P computes the PCP indices Q that VPCP (x; r) would
query, generates a Merkle opening proof pf for π[Q], and
sends the response z := (π[Q], pf) to V .3

accepted by the PCP veriﬁer VPCP (x; r). Kilian’s protocol is
publicly veriﬁable: one can compute whether V accepts given
the instance x and the transcript (hCRHF , cm, r, z).

D. A closer look at Unruh’s lemma
Unruh’s lemma is a quantum information-theoretic statement about any collection of binary-outcome projective measurements {Ar }r∈R . We write binary-outcome projective measurements as Ar = (Πr , I − Πr ) where Πr is associated with
outcome 1, and I − Πr with outcome 0.
Let MixM({Ar }r ) be the corresponding mixture of the projective measurements {Ar }r , i.e., the procedure that chooses
r ← R uniformly at random, applies measurement Ar , and
outputs the outcome b ∈ {0, 1}. Unruh’s lemma [2], [4]
concerns the measurement outcomes obtained from sequential
applications of MixM({Ar }r ).

equivocal hash function:10 a hash function that is collision
resistant, but where one can break the security of the hash
function as a commitment scheme. For example, it is possible
to send a hash image y, and then upon receiving an arbitrary
preﬁx z, “open” that image to a pre-image x of y with preﬁx
z. Equivocal hash functions do not exist classically, due to a
rewinding argument, but Ambainis et al. [14] construct them
relative to a quantum oracle. Amos et al. [17] later give a
construction relative to a classical oracle.
While Ambainis et al. use equivocal hash functions to
give unsound interactive proofs, the results do not immediately apply to the case of Kilian’s protocol. This is because
Merkle trees do not necessarily preserve equivocality of the
component hash function. In particular, equivocating Merkle
trees would seem to require equivocating the underlying hash
function on either the left half or the right half of the input.
On the other hand, only a very short preﬁx can be equivocated
in the existing works. (Ambanis et al. allow for a richer class
of equivocations than just preﬁxes, but they must still be short
relative to the input length.)
Nevertheless, we observe that a slight variant of Merkle
trees does preserve the equivocality of the underlying hash
function. Namely, if each node is obtained by hashing the
children together with an arbitrarily long auxiliary string. By
setting the length of the auxiliary strings sufﬁciently long,
one can equivocate on a preﬁx long enough to arbitrarily
choose the child nodes. This allows for full equivocality
of Merkle trees, while still preserving collision resistance.
More generally, it yields a vector commitment that is collision
resistant, but equivocal and therefore insufﬁcient for the postquantum security of Kilian’s protocol.
We leave as an interesting open question whether Kilian’s
protocol instantiated with unmodiﬁed Merkle trees using a
post-quantum CRHF is sufﬁcient for post-quantum security.
We note, however, that if Kilian’s protocol instantiated with
a CRHF is not post-quantum secure, then it means that the
CRHF is not collapsing. As shown by Zhandry [18], such
a CRHF would yield strong cryptographic objects, namely
“quantum lightning”, which have no known instantiations
under well-studied assumptions. (More precisely, Zhandry [18]
shows that non-collapsing CRHFs imply inﬁnitely-often secure
quantum lightning, a slightly weaker notion.)

H. Quantum strategies for repeated games
Our quantum rewinding techniques can be cast in the
language of single-player games, where a referee asks a player
a random question r ← R, the player responds with an
answer z, and wins if f (r, z) = 1 for some predicate f .
Mapped onto this setting, the quantum rewinding task is to
transform any efﬁcient quantum strategy for winning the game
once into an efﬁcient strategy that wins in many instances of
an n-fold sequential repetition of this game, where in each
repetition the referee only measures whether the player has
won. Importantly, we are only given one copy of the quantum
state used by the one-time strategy.
In the context of rewinding, we set f (r, z) := V (τ, r, z) to
be the veriﬁer predicate with partial transcript τ . The strategy
of the prover in the last round of the protocol is then an
efﬁcient strategy for the one-time game. To obtain multiple
accepting transcripts, a rewinding extractor plays the sequential repetition of the game. Note that by measuring Z in the
computational basis if the player has won, the extractor obtains
an accepting response z; the protocol’s collapsing property
ensures that this additional measurement is not detectable by
an efﬁcient strategy.
This gives a conceptually simple characterization of the
quantum rewinding task, which may be of independent interest. In the full version [16], we develop general techniques
that apply to any single-player game.

I. Discussion: is collapsing necessary for Kilian’s protocol?
Since collision-resistant hash functions (CRHFs) sufﬁce in
the classical setting, a natural question is whether Kilian’s
protocol (in its original formulation using Merkle trees) is
post-quantum secure when instantiated with any post-quantum
CRHF. We do not know the answer, but believe that the existing evidence points to collision resistance being insufﬁcient
for Kilian’s protocol.
